paras: The lynching of William Stokes was the killing of a Black farm laborer who was shot dead after being taken from a constable's custody near Marmora, Dinwiddie County, Virginia, in June 1888. Stokes had been arrested on a charge arising from alleged entries into houses on the farm where he had worked, and his body was found in a road a short distance from where he had been held. A coroner's jury found that he had been shot by persons unknown, and in August a Dinwiddie grand jury dismissed the matter for lack of evidence. Virginia papers treated the case as a lynching carried out with such secrecy that no one was ever suspected.

According to the Petersburg correspondent of the Richmond Dispatch, Stokes was about twenty-five to twenty-seven years old and a "comparative stranger" who had arrived in the neighborhood around the first of April looking for work. He was hired on the farm of J. M. Abernathy, though no one could say where he came from; the last report was that he was from near Norfolk. The correspondent wrote that it was "stated" that Stokes had several times broken into Abernathy's house "with intentions, it is believed, other than robbery," and that he was driven out and later discharged. He was further alleged to have forced his way into the house of a Black tenant on the same farm, where an assault on the tenant's daughter was suspected. Warned to leave the county, he reportedly answered that "this was a game at which two could play."

The Petersburg Index-Appeal, as reprinted in the Martinsburg Independent, said Stokes was arrested on a Saturday on a warrant charging him with breaking into Abernathy's dwelling and was placed in the charge of Special Constable Gresham. Because some witnesses were absent, a justice of the peace continued the hearing until Monday, and Gresham took the prisoner to his own house, locked him in a corn-crib and gave him a bed. The Dispatch's August report gave a different charge, entering the tenant's house "with the intention of committing an assault," and said Stokes was locked in a farm-house until he could be taken to the county jail.

In the Index-Appeal's account, Gresham went to the crib on Monday morning, found the doors open and the prisoner gone, and about an hour later learned that a dead man lay down the road. He identified the body as Stokes, who had been shot in the back and in the back of the neck. The Richmond Dispatch, by contrast, said the body was found on Sunday morning and later dated the lynching to Saturday night, June 16, about fifteen miles west of Petersburg near the Appomattox River.

A coroner's inquest returned a verdict that Stokes had died from being shot "by some one to them unknown." The Dispatch's correspondent wrote that the affair was "so well conducted" that no one was suspected, and that it was not known whether the lynching party was white or Black. The County Court referred the case to the grand jury, though the correspondent expected nothing definite to come of it. On August 20 the Dinwiddie grand jury tried to identify those involved, could obtain no evidence against anyone, and dismissed the matter.

The Richmond Dispatch printed its correspondent's letter of June 21 under the headlines "SUPPOSED LYNCHING" and "A NEORO'S [Negro's] MYSTERIOUS DEATH IN DIN- WIDDIE," and the Alexandria Gazette ran a shortened version of the same text that day. Both said there seemed "to be no doubt" that Stokes had died by lynching, while presenting the charges against him as hearsay, introduced with "It is stated" and "It is further alleged." The Index-Appeal's account, carried in West Virginia as "A Mysterious Murder in Virginia," called the killing a murder, did not use the word lynching, and dwelt on the custody arrangements and the inquest.

Further afield, the Russellville Democrat gave the case one paragraph in its "Southern Gleanings" column, describing the charge as "criminal assault" and noting that the constable had first assumed Stokes had escaped. Two months later the Dispatch headed its grand-jury report "THE DINWIDDIE LYNCHING CASE" and described the affair as "wrapped in the utmost secrecy."

reader.title: Lynching of William Stokes
bases: Stokes, a prisoner held by a constable on a criminal charge, was taken from where he was confined and shot dead by unknown persons, which the Richmond Dispatch called a lynching (A3, A4, A6).

Stokes was shot dead after being removed from a constable's custody while awaiting a hearing on a criminal charge, and the Dispatch spoke of a 'lynching party' (A3, A4, A6); but no witness saw the killers, the coroner's jury found only that he was shot 'by some one to them unknown', and the number of killers is never given (A4).

The Richmond Dispatch's Petersburg correspondent (A3, A6) and the Petersburg Index-Appeal as reprinted in A4 independently report the arrest, the disappearance from custody and the shooting, with A2 and A5 condensing the same accounts.

accounts.label: Richmond Dispatch Petersburg correspondent (June)
accounts.gist: Stokes, accused of night entries into Abernathy's house and the tenant's house, was by 'prevailing impression' taken from his 'prison-house' and shot by unknown parties; the lynching was so well managed no one was suspected.

accounts.label: Petersburg Index-Appeal
accounts.gist: Arrested Saturday on a warrant for breaking into Abernathy's house, Stokes was held in Constable Gresham's corn-crib pending a Monday hearing; Monday morning the crib was open and his body, shot in the back and neck, lay down the road; a coroner's jury blamed persons unknown.

accounts.label: Richmond Dispatch (August, grand jury)
accounts.gist: Arrested for entering the tenant's house intending an assault and locked in a farm-house, Stokes was found shot the next morning; the grand jury found no evidence and dismissed the matter.

framing.detail: Headed 'SUPPOSED LYNCHING. A NEORO'S MYSTERIOUS DEATH'; states the accusations as allegations and stresses that the lynchers left no trace, without comment on the killing.
Headed 'A Mysterious Murder in Virginia'; a factual account of custody, wounds and inquest that calls it murder, not lynching.
One-paragraph item among regional news briefs, giving the charge as 'criminal assault'.
Headed 'THE DINWIDDIE LYNCHING CASE'; reports the grand jury's failure and the 'utmost secrecy' of the affair.
